chunks: There was a man in the mosque of al-Medina speaking about al-Qadar while people were gathering around him. So I said to him, 'O you, I want to question you.' He said, 'Ask.' I said, 'Can there be in the kingdom of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, that which He does not will?' He lowered his head for a long time, then raised his head toward me and said to me: 'O you! If I say that there does happen to be in His kingdom what He does not will, then He is indeed subdued; and if I say that there cannot be in His kingdom except what He wills, I would be admitting to you (the right to commit) disobedience.'

He (the narrator) said: So I told Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'I asked this Qadari, and his answer was such and such.' So he (the Imam) said: 'He looked out for himself. But had he said other than what he said, he would have been destroyed.'

key_terms.الْقَدَر: al-Qadar: divine pre-determination or decree; the doctrine that God has foreknowledge and ordains all events
key_terms.الْقَدَرِيَّ: al-Qadari: one who holds that humans have complete free will independent of divine determination; often used polemically
key_terms.الْمَعَاصِي: al-ma'asi: acts of disobedience, sins; the theological problem being that if God wills everything, He would will sins too
key_terms.مَقْهُورٌ: maqhur: overpowered, subdued; the implication being that a god whose will can be overridden is not truly omnipotent

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the Qadari who evaded the dilemma of divine will and human disobedience?
ai.summary: Ismail ibn Jabir recounts challenging a Qadari theologian in Medina with a classic dilemma about divine will: if anything can happen contrary to Allah's will, Allah is overpowered; if nothing happens except what Allah wills, then sins are also willed, implying God endorses disobedience. The Qadari avoided both horns of the dilemma through evasion. When Ismail reported this to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the Imam acknowledged the man's shrewdness in avoiding theological self-destruction — for an inadequate answer on this question would constitute heresy (and thus 'destruction'). This is the classical antinomy at the heart of the free will vs. divine sovereignty debate that occupied early Islamic kalam (speculative theology). The Shia position — 'the matter is between the two matters' (al-amr bayna al-amrayn) — resolves this by affirming both divine sovereignty and human moral agency without collapsing into either Jabriyya (absolute compulsion) or Qadariyya (absolute free will).

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Usman Bin Isa, from Ismail Bin Jabir who said, 
‘There was a man in a Masjid of Al-Medina who was speaking regarding the Pre-determination, and the people were gathering. So I said, ‘O you! I (would like to) question you’. He said, ‘Ask’. I said, ‘Can there happen to be in the Kingdom of Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Blessed and High what He<sup>azwj</sup> does not want?’ So he lowered his head for a long while, then raised his head towards me, so he said to me, ‘O you! If I were to say that there does happen to be in His<sup>azwj</sup> Kingdom what He<sup>azwj</sup> does not want, so He<sup>azwj</sup> would be defeated, and if I were to say that there cannot happen to be in His<sup>azwj</sup> Kingdom except what He<sup>azwj</sup> wants, I would be acknowledging to you with the disobedience (freedom to commit sins)’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘I said to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘I asked the Qadiriyya, so it was from his answers, such and such’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘He watched out for himself. But, had he said other than what he said, he would be destroyed’.
